The thorn, the head of one of the courses of the priests ([1 Chr. 24:10](#1Chr.24.10)).

Warm, hot, and hence the south; also an Egyptian word meaning “black”, the youngest son of Noah ([Gen. 5:32](#Gen.5.32); comp. 9:22, 24). The curse pronounced by Noah against Ham, properly against Canaan his fourth son, was accomplished when the Jews subsequently exterminated the Canaanites.

(of Persian origin), magnificent, the name of the vizier (i.e., the prime minister) of the Persian king Ahasuerus ([Esther 3:1](#Esth.3.1), etc.). He is called an “Agagite,” which seems to denote that he was descended from the royal family of the Amalekites, the bitterest enemies of the Jews, as Agag was one of the titles of the Amalekite kings. He or his parents were brought to Persia as captives taken in war. He was hanged on the gallows which he had erected for Mordecai the Jew ([Esther 7:10](#Esth.7.10)).
Father of Haman, designated usually “the Agagite” ([Esther 3:1](#Esth.3.1), [10](#Esth.3.10); [8:5](#Esth.8.5)).

The king’s, the father of Jerahmeel, mentioned in [Jer. 36:26](#Jer.36.26). Some take this word as a common noun, “the king”, and understand that Jerahmeel was Jehoiakim’s son. Probably, however, it is to be taken as a proper name.
The queen, the daughter of Machir and sister of Gilead ([1 Chr. 7:17](#1Chr.7.17), [18](#1Chr.7.18)). Abiezer was one of her three children.

He-ass, a Hivite from whom Jacob purchased the plot of ground in which Joseph was afterwards buried ([Gen. 33:19](#Gen.33.19)). He is called “Emmor” in [Acts 7:16](#Acts.7.16). His son Shechem founded the city of that name which Simeon and Levi destroyed because of his crime in the matter of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter ([Gen. 34:20](#Gen.34.20)). Hamor and Shechem were also slain (ver. 26).
Spared, one of the sons of Pharez, son of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:5](#1Chr.2.5)). His descendants are called Hamulites ([Num. 26:21](#Num.26.21)).
Kinsman of the dew, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, wife of king Josiah, and mother of king Jehoahaz ([2 Kings 23:31](#2Kgs.23.31)), also of king Zedekiah ([2 Kings 24:18](#2Kgs.24.18)).
Whom God has graciously given, the cousin of Jeremiah, to whom he sold the field he possessed in Anathoth, before the siege of Jerusalem ([Jer. 32:6-12](#Jer.32.6)).
One of the Levites who assisted Ezra ([Neh. 8:7](#Neh.8.7)).
One of the chiefs who subscribed the covenant ([Neh. 10:22](#Neh.10.22)).

A prophet who was sent to rebuke king Asa for entering into a league with Benhadad I., king of Syria, against Judah ([2 Chr. 16:1-10](#2Chr.16.1)). He was probably the father of the prophet Jehu ([1 Kings 16:7](#1Kgs.16.7)).
One of the sons of Heman ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4), [25](#1Chr.25.25)).
Probably a brother of Nehemiah ([Neh. 1:2](#Neh.1.2); [7:2](#Neh.7.2)), who reported to him the melancholy condition of Jerusalem. Nehemiah afterwards appointed him to have charge of the city gates.
One of the sons of Heman ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4), [23](#1Chr.25.23)).
A chief of the tribe of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 8:24](#1Chr.8.24)).
One of Uzziah’s military officers ([2 Chr. 26:11](#2Chr.26.11)).
The “ruler of the palace; he was a faithful man, and feared God above many” ([Neh. 7:2](#Neh.7.2)).
Grandfather of the captain who arrested Jeremiah ([Jer. 37:13](#Jer.37.13)).
A chief of the tribe of Asher ([1 Chr. 7:39](#1Chr.7.39)).

Favour, grace, one of the wives of Elkanah the Levite, and the mother of Samuel ([1 Sam. 1](#1Sam.1); [2](#1Sam.2)). Her home was at Ramathaim-zophim, whence she was wont every year to go to Shiloh, where the tabernacle had been pitched by Joshua, to attend the offering of sacrifices there according to the law ([Ex. 23:15](#Exod.23.15); [34:18](#Exod.34.18); [Deut. 16:16](#Deut.16.16)), probably at the feast of the Passover (comp. [Ex. 13:10](#Exod.13.10)). On occasion of one of these “yearly” visits, being grieved by reason of Peninnah’s conduct toward her, she went forth alone, and kneeling before the Lord at the sanctuary she prayed inaudibly. …
A chief of the tribe of Manasseh ([Num. 34:23](#Num.34.23)).

The son and successor of Nahash, king of Moab. David’s messengers, sent on an embassy of condolence to him to Rabbah Ammon, his capital, were so grossly insulted that he proclaimed war against Hanun. David’s army, under the command of Joab, forthwith crossed the Jordan, and gained a complete victory over the Moabites and their allies ([2 Sam. 10:1-14](#2Sam.10.1)) at Medeba (q.v.).

Heb. haran; i.e., “mountaineer.” The eldest son of Terah, brother of Abraham and Nahor, and father of Lot, Milcah, and Iscah. He died before his father ([Gen. 11:27](#Gen.11.27)), in Ur of the Chaldees.
The son of Caleb of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:46](#1Chr.2.46)) by his concubine Ephah.
(a Persian word meaning “ass-driver”), one of the seven eunuchs or chamberlains of king Ahasuerus ([Esther 1:10](#Esth.1.10); [7:9](#Esth.7.9)).
Zeal of Jehovah, ([Neh. 3:8](#Neh.3.8)) “of the goldsmiths,” one whose son helped to repair the wall of Jerusalem.
The head of the second course of priests ([1 Chr. 24:8](#1Chr.24.8)).
A chief of the tribe of Asher ([1 Chr. 7:36](#1Chr.7.36)).
Worker or enchanter, one of the Nethinim ([Ezra 2:52](#Ezra.2.52); [Neh. 7:54](#Neh.7.54)).
Elevated, ([1 Chr. 4:8](#1Chr.4.8)), a descendant of Judah.
Eager, the father of Meshullemeth, the wife of king Manasseh ([2 Kings 21:19](#2Kgs.21.19)) and mother of king Amon.
Favoured by Jehovah, one of the sons of Pedaiah ([1 Chr. 3:20](#1Chr.3.20)), of the royal line of David.
Bristling or hated, a Benjamite ([1 Chr. 9:7](#1Chr.9.7)).
One of the chief priests in the time of Ezra ([Ezra 8:24](#Ezra.8.24)).
One of the chief Levites ([2 Chr. 35:9](#2Chr.35.9)).
One of the Levites whom Ezra appointed to interpret the law to the people ([Neh. 9:5](#Neh.9.5)).
Consideration in judging, stood at Ezra’s left hand when he read the law ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
Ibid., a descendant of David ([1 Chr. 3:20](#1Chr.3.20)).
Stood on Ezra’s left hand while he read the law ([Neh. 8:4](#Neh.8.4)).
Poverty, “keeper of the wardrobe,” i.e., of the sacerdotal vestments ([2 Chr. 34:22](#2Chr.34.22)); called Harhas [2 Kings 22:14](#2Kgs.22.14). He was husband of the prophetess Huldah.
A Levite of the family of Merari ([Neh. 11:15](#Neh.11.15); [1 Chr. 9:14](#1Chr.9.14)).
Verity, one of the eunuchs or chamberlains in the palace of Ahasuerus ([Esther 4:5](#Esth.4.5), [6](#Esth.4.6), [9](#Esth.4.9), [10](#Esth.4.10)).
Exploration, one of the temple porters or janitors ([Ezra 2:42](#Ezra.2.42)). He returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
A priest who returned with Zerubbabel ([Neh. 12:2](#Neh.12.2)).
One of the sons of Cush ([Gen. 10:7](#Gen.10.7)).

Whom God beholds, an officer of Ben-hadad II., king of Syria, who ultimately came to the throne, according to the word of the Lord to Elijah ([1 Kings 19:15](#1Kgs.19.15)), after he had put the king to death ([2 Kings 8:15](#2Kgs.8.15)). His interview with Elisha is mentioned in [2 Kings 8](#2Kgs.8). The Assyrians soon after his accession to the throne came against him and defeated him with very great loss; and three years afterwards again invaded Syria, but on this occasion Hazael submitted to them. …

Court of death, the third son of Joktan, and a region in Arabia-Felix settled by him ([Gen. 10:26](#Gen.10.26); [1 Chr. 1:20](#1Chr.1.20)). It is probably the modern province of Hadramaut, situated on the Indian Ocean east of the modern Yemen.
Vision, one of the sons of Nahor ([Gen. 22:22](#Gen.22.22)).
Son of Beriah and grandson of Asher ([Gen. 46:17](#Gen.46.17); [1 Chr. 7:31](#1Chr.7.31), [32](#1Chr.7.32)).
The Kenite ([Judg. 4:11](#Judg.4.11), [17](#Judg.4.17); 5:24), a descendant of Hobab. His wife Jael received Sisera (q.v.) into her tent and then killed him.
One of the seven heads of the families of the Gadites ([1 Chr. 5:13](#1Chr.5.13)).
The third son of Kohath the Levite ([Ex. 6:18](#Exod.6.18); [1 Chr. 6:2](#1Chr.6.2), [18](#1Chr.6.18)).
Eunuch, had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus ([Esther 2:8](#Esth.2.8)).
Rust, ([1 Chr. 4:5](#1Chr.4.5), [7](#1Chr.4.7)), one of the wives of Ashur.
Fatness, one of David’s warriors ([2 Sam. 23:29](#2Sam.23.29)).
Elevation, father of Joseph in the line of our Lord’s ancestry ([Luke 3:23](#Luke.3.23)).
Smooth-tongued, one of the chief priests in the time of Joiakim ([Neh. 12:15](#Neh.12.15)).
Strong, father of Eliab, who was “captain of the children of Zebulun” ([Num. 1:9](#Num.1.9); [2:7](#Num.2.7)).

Grandson of Samuel ([1 Chr. 6:33](#1Chr.6.33); [15:17](#1Chr.15.17)), to whom the 88th Psalm probably was inscribed. He was one of the “seers” named in [2 Chr. 29:14](#2Chr.29.14), [30](#2Chr.29.30), and took a leading part in the administration of the sacred services.
[1 Kings 4:31](#1Kgs.4.31); [1 Chr. 2:6](#1Chr.2.6), a son of Zerah, noted for his wisdom.
[1 Kings 4:31](#1Kgs.4.31); [1 Chr. 2:6](#1Chr.2.6), a son of Zerah, noted for his wisdom.
Favour of Hadad, the name of a Levite after the Captivity ([Ezra 3:9](#Ezra.3.9)).
The second son of Asher ([1 Chr. 4:6](#1Chr.4.6)).

Mercury-born, at one time Paul’s fellow-labourer in Asia Minor, who, however, afterwards abandoned him, along with one Phygellus, probably on account of the perils by which they were beset ([2 Tim. 1:15](#2Tim.1.15)).

Son of Aristobulus and Bernice, and grandson of Herod the Great. He was made tetrarch of the provinces formerly held by Lysanias II., and ultimately possessed the entire kingdom of his grandfather, Herod the Great, with the title of king. He put the apostle James the elder to death, and cast Peter into prison ([Luke 3:1](#Luke.3.1); [Acts 12:1-19](#Acts.12.1)). On the second day of a festival held in honour of the emperor Claudius, he appeared in the great theatre of Caesarea. “The king came in clothed in magnificent robes, of which silver was the costly brilliant material. …

([Matt. 14:3-11](#Matt.14.3); [Mark 6:17-28](#Mark.6.17); [Luke 3:19](#Luke.3.19)), the daughter of Aristobulus and Bernice. While residing at Rome with her husband Herod Philip I. and her daughter, Herod Antipas fell in with her during one of his journeys to that city. She consented to leave her husband and become his wife. Some time after, Herod met John the Baptist, who boldly declared the marriage to be unlawful. For this he was “cast into prison,” in the castle probably of Machaerus (q.v.), and was there subsequently beheaded.
A Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes and calls his “kinsman” ([Rom. 16:11](#Rom.16.11)).

Dread, a descendant of Canaan, and the ancestor of the Hittites ([Gen. 10:18](#Gen.10.18); [Deut. 7:1](#Deut.7.1)), who dwelt in the vicinity of Hebron ([Gen. 23:3](#Gen.23.3), [7](#Gen.23.7)). The Hittites were a Hamitic race. They are called “the sons of Heth” ([Gen. 23:3](#Gen.23.3), [5](#Gen.23.5), [7](#Gen.23.7), [10](#Gen.23.10), [16](#Gen.23.16), [18](#Gen.23.18), [20](#Gen.23.20)).

Son of Ahaz ([2 Kings 18:1](#2Kgs.18.1); [2 Chr. 29:1](#2Chr.29.1)), whom he succeeded on the throne of the kingdom of Judah. He reigned twenty-nine years (B.C. 726-697). The history of this king is contained in [2 Kings 18:20](#2Kgs.18.20), [Isa. 36](#Isa.36)-39, and [2 Chr. 29](#2Chr.29)-32. He is spoken of as a great and good king. In public life he followed the example of his great-granfather Uzziah. He set himself to abolish idolatry from his kingdom, and among other things which he did for this end, he destroyed the “brazen serpent,” which had been removed to Jerusalem, and had become an object of idolatrous worship ([Num. 21:9](#Num.21.9)). A great reformation was wrought in the kingdom of Judah in his day ([2 Kings 18:4](#2Kgs.18.4); [2 Chr. 29:3-36](#2Chr.29.3)).
Vision, the father of Tabrimon, and grandfather of Ben-hadad, king of Syria ([1 Kings 15:18](#1Kgs.15.18)).
The head of the seventeenth course of the priests ([1 Chr. 24:15](#1Chr.24.15)).
A Carmelite, one of David’s warriors ([1 Chr. 11:37](#1Chr.11.37)).
The older of the two sons of Pharez ([Gen. 46:12](#Gen.46.12)).
One of the sons of Reuben ([Gen. 46:9](#Gen.46.9); [Ex. 6:14](#Exod.6.14)).

Life of (i.e., from) God, a native of Bethel, who built (i.e., fortified) Jericho some seven hundred years after its destruction by the Israelites. There fell on him for such an act the imprecation of Joshua (6:26). He laid the foundation in his first-born, and set up the gates in his youngest son ([1 Kings 16:34](#1Kgs.16.34)), i.e., during the progress of the work all his children died.

The high priest in the reign of Josiah ([1 Chr. 6:13](#1Chr.6.13); [Ezra 7:1](#Ezra.7.1)). To him and his deputy ([2 Kings 23:5](#2Kgs.23.5)), along with the ordinary priests and the Levites who had charge of the gates, was entrusted the purification of the temple in Jerusalem. While this was in progress, he discovered in some hidden corner of the building a book called the “book of the law” ([2 Kings 22:8](#2Kgs.22.8)) and the “book of the covenant” (23:2). Some have supposed that this “book” was nothing else than the original autograph copy of the Pentateuch written by Moses ([Deut. 31:9-26](#Deut.31.9)). This remarkable discovery occurred in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign (B.C. 624), a discovery which permanently affected the whole subsequent history of Israel.
Praising, a Pirathonite, father of the judge Abdon ([Judg. 12:13](#Judg.12.13), [15](#Judg.12.15)).

Also “Huram” and “Horam,” king of Tyre. He entered into an alliance with David, and assisted him in building his palace by sending him able workmen, and also cedar-trees and fir-trees from Lebanon ([2 Sam. 5:11](#2Sam.5.11); [1 Chr. 14:1](#1Chr.14.1)). After the death of David he entered into a similar alliance with Solomon, and assisted him greatly in building the temple ([1 Kings 5:1](#1Kgs.5.1); [9:11](#1Kgs.9.11); [2 Chr. 2:3](#2Chr.2.3)). He also took part in Solomon’s traffic to the Eastern Seas ([1 Kings 9:27](#1Kgs.9.27); [10:11](#1Kgs.10.11); [2 Chr. 8:18](#2Chr.8.18); [9:10](#2Chr.9.10)).

The “master workman” whom Hiram sent to Solomon. He was the son of a widow of Dan, and of a Tyrian father. In [2 Chr. 2:13](#2Chr.2.13) “Huram my father” should be Huram Abi, the word “Abi” (rendered here “my father”) being regarded as a proper name, or it may perhaps be a title of distinction given to Huram, and equivalent to “master.” (Comp. [1 Kings 7:14](#1Kgs.7.14); [2 Chr. 4:16](#2Chr.4.16).) He cast the magnificent brazen works for Solomon’s temple in clay-beds in the valley of Jordan, between Succoth and Zarthan.

One of the original tribes scattered over Palestine, from Hermon to Gibeon in the south. The name is interpreted as “midlanders” or “villagers” ([Gen. 10:17](#Gen.10.17); [1 Chr. 1:15](#1Chr.1.15)). They were probably a branch of the Hittites. At the time of Jacob’s return to Canaan, Hamor the Hivite was the “prince of the land” ([Gen. 24:2-28](#Gen.24.2)).

Beloved, the Kenite, has been usually identified with Jethro (q.v.), [Ex. 18:5](#Exod.18.5), [27](#Exod.18.27); comp. [Num. 10:29](#Num.10.29), [30](#Num.10.30). In [Judg. 4:11](#Judg.4.11), the word rendered “father-in-law” means properly any male relative by marriage (comp. [Gen. 19:14](#Gen.19.14), “son-in-law,” A.V.), and should be rendered “brother-in-law,” as in the R.V. His descendants followed Israel to Canaan ([Num. 10:29](#Num.10.29)), and at first pitched their tents near Jericho, but afterwards settled in the south in the borders of Arad ([Judg. 1:8-11](#Judg.1.8), [16](#Judg.1.16)).
One of the Levites who assisted Ezra in expounding the law ([Neh. 8:7](#Neh.8.7); [9:5](#Neh.9.5)).
[Neh. 10:18](#Neh.10.18), a Levite who sealed the covenant.
Partridge, one of the daughters of Zelophehad the Gileadite, to whom portions were assigned by Moses ([Num. 26:33](#Num.26.33); [27:1](#Num.27.1); [36:11](#Num.36.11)).
Jehovah impels, the king of Hebron who joined the league against Gibeon. He and his allies were defeated ([Josh. 10:3](#Josh.10.3), [5](#Josh.10.5), [16](#Josh.10.16)-27).
The third Person of the adorable Trinity.

Pugilist or client, one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest ([1 Sam. 1:3](#1Sam.1.3); [2:34](#1Sam.2.34)), who, because he was “very old,” resigned to them the active duties of his office. By their scandalous conduct they brought down a curse on their father’s house (2:22, 12-27, 27-36; 3:11-14). For their wickedness they were called “sons of Belial,” i.e., worthless men (2:12). They both perished in the disastrous battle with the Philistines at Aphek (4:11).
A Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 16:38](#1Chr.16.38)).

Salvation, the son of Beeri, and author of the book of prophecies bearing his name. He belonged to the kingdom of Israel. “His Israelitish origin is attested by the peculiar, rough, Aramaizing diction, pointing to the northern part of Palestine; by the intimate acquaintance he evinces with the localities of Ephraim (5:1; 6:8, 9; 12:12; 14:6, etc.); by passages like 1:2, where the kingdom is styled ‘the land’, and 7:5, where the Israelitish king is designated as ‘our’ king.” The period of his ministry (extending to some sixty years) is indicated in the superscription ([Hos. 1:1](#Hos.1.1), [2](#Hos.1.2)). He is the only prophet of Israel who has left any written prophecy.

The last king of Israel. He conspired against and slew his predecessor, Pekah ([Isa. 7:16](#Isa.7.16)), but did not ascend the throne till after an interregnum of warfare of eight years ([2 Kings 17:1](#2Kgs.17.1), [2](#2Kgs.17.2)). Soon after this he submitted to Shalmaneser, the Assyrian king, who a second time invaded the land to punish Hoshea, because of his withholding tribute which he had promised to pay. A second revolt brought back the Assyrian king Sargon, who besieged Samaria, and carried the ten tribes away beyond the Euphrates, B.C. 720 ([2 Kings 17:5](#2Kgs.17.5), [6](#2Kgs.17.6); 18:9-12). No more is heard of Hoshea. He disappeared like “foam upon the water” ([Hos. 10:7](#Hos.10.7); [13:11](#Hos.13.11)).
[1 Chr. 27:20](#1Chr.27.20). The ruler of Ephraim in David’s time.
A stroke, great-grandson of Asher ([1 Chr. 7:35](#1Chr.7.35)).
Circle, the second son of Aram ([Gen. 10:23](#Gen.10.23)), and grandson of Shem.

Weasel, a prophetess; the wife of Shallum. She was consulted regarding the “book of the law” discovered by the high priest Hilkiah ([2 Kings 22:14-20](#2Kgs.22.14); [2 Chr. 34:22-28](#2Chr.34.22)). She resided in that part of Jerusalem called the Mishneh (A.V., “the college;” R.V., “the second quarter”), supposed by some to be the suburb between the inner and the outer wall, the second or lower city, Akra. Miriam ([Ex. 15:20](#Exod.15.20)) and Deborah ([Judg. 4:4](#Judg.4.4)) are the only others who bear the title of “prophetess,” for the word in [Isa. 8:3](#Isa.8.3) means only the prophet’s wife.

The husband of Miriam, Moses’ sister ([Ex. 17:10-12](#Exod.17.10)). He was associated with Aaron in charge of the people when Moses was absent on Sinai ([Ex. 24:14](#Exod.24.14)). He was probably of the tribe of Judah, and grandfather of Bezaleel ([Ex. 31:2](#Exod.31.2); [35:30](#Exod.35.30); [1 Chr. 2:19](#1Chr.2.19)).
One of the five princes of Midian who were defeated and slain by the Israelites under the command of Phinehas ([Num. 31:8](#Num.31.8)).
Linen-worker, one of David’s heroes, a native of the valley of Mount Gaash ([1 Chr. 11:32](#1Chr.11.32)).
Generally “Huram,” one of the sons of Bela ([1 Chr. 8:5](#1Chr.8.5)).

Quick, “the Archite,” “the king’s friend” ([1 Chr. 27:33](#1Chr.27.33)). When David fled from Jerusalem, on account of the rebellion of Absalom, and had reached the summit of Olivet, he there met Hushai, whom he sent back to Jerusalem for the purpose of counteracting the influence of Ahithophel, who had joined the ranks of Absalom ([2 Sam. 15:32](#2Sam.15.32), [37](#2Sam.15.37); 16:16-18). It was by his advice that Absalom refrained from immediately pursuing after David. By this delay the cause of Absalom was ruined, for it gave David time to muster his forces.
Chosen, one of David’s sons ([1 Chr. 3:6](#1Chr.3.6); [2 Sam. 5:15](#2Sam.5.15)).
Illustrious, the tenth judge of Israel ([Judg. 12:8-10](#Judg.12.8)). He ruled seven years.
Lovely. A prophet of Judah who wrote the history of Rehoboam and Abijah ([2 Chr. 12:15](#2Chr.12.15)). He has been identified with Oded ([2 Chr. 15:1](#2Chr.15.1)).
Timely. The father of Ahinadab, who was one of Solomon’s purveyors ([1 Kings 4:14](#1Kgs.4.14)).
Lovely. The son of Zechariah ([1 Chr. 27:21](#1Chr.27.21)), the ruler of Manasseh in David’s time.
[Num. 13:7](#Num.13.7), one of the spies of the tribe of Issachar.
Son of Nathan of Zobah, and one of David’s warriors ([2 Sam. 23:36](#2Sam.23.36)).
An Ahohite, one of David’s chief warriors ([1 Chr. 11:29](#1Chr.11.29)); called also Zalmon ([2 Sam. 23:28](#2Sam.23.28)).
Replenisher, the father of Micaiah the prophet ([2 Chr. 18:7](#2Chr.18.7), [8](#2Chr.18.8)).
The head of the sixteenth priestly order ([1 Chr. 24:14](#1Chr.24.14)).
